item.title: QNAP Warns Users as Plex2Shell Flaws Are Used to Hack NAS Devices
item.description:
Taiwanese vendor QNAP urges users to update Plex Media Server after reports of NAS compromises through the Plex2Shell vulnerability chain.

QNAP urges users to update Plex Media Server through the QNAP App Center after reports that threat actors exploited the Plex2Shell vulnerability chain to compromise NAS devices.

“QNAP has received reports from some users that Plex Media Server on their NAS appears to have been compromised through these vulnerabilities, and QNAP Technical Support is assisting the affected usersadvisory published by QNAP. ” reads the report published by the vendor. “The QNAP Product Security Incident Response Team (QNAP PSIRT) has confirmed that the vulnerabilities exist only in Plex Media Server; QTS, QuTS hero, and other QNAP operating systems are not themselves affected.”

Plex Media Server is designed to make movies, music, and other media available across devices. But when a server is exposed to the internet and runs vulnerable software, it can become an entry point for attackers who have little interest in your film collection.

On October 16, 2026, security researcher Zach Main published technical details and proof-of-concept (PoC) code for a vulnerability chain dubbed Plex2Shell. Within a day, researchers had observed attackers using the exploit against an internet-facing honeypot, deploying cryptocurrency-mining malware and proxy software. The incident is a reminder of how quickly a public exploit can be weaponized by threat actors.

The chain combines four vulnerabilities in Plex Media Server: CVE-2026-96652, CVE-2026-96654, CVE-2026-96655, and CVE-2026-96656. Together, they can allow attackers to execute arbitrary code on vulnerable servers without valid credentials, provided the required conditions are met. The code runs with the privileges of the Plex service, giving attackers an opportunity to install additional software and abuse the host.

The technical details are available in Main’s original analysis, Plex2Shell. Plex had been notified of the vulnerabilities on July 27 and acknowledged the report on August 4, awarding a bug bounty. The company released fixes in September, before the exploit code became public.

The loader does not check the library’s name, executable permissions, digital signature, or symbols. As a result, the library’s ELF constructor can run with the same privileges as the Plex service.

“It doesn’t check for a lib prefix, doesn’t require the execute bit, doesn’t verify any signature, and doesn’t look for any specific symbol.” reads the report published by zmain.com. “When dlopen loads a shared object, it runs the ELF’s DT_INIT_ARRAY (constructor functions) before doing any symbol resolution. A .so that only has a constructor and no exported symbols will still execute its code on load. We then trigger a second transcode. The codec directory gets re-enumerated, the .so we wrote in Stage 4 gets loaded, and the constructor runs as uid=1000(plex).”

That detail matters because the final stage can exploit how Plex loads shared libraries. The chain uses a setting related to transcoding to influence execution, allowing a specially crafted library to run when Plex loads it. The result can be code execution under the service account, without requiring the attacker to obtain an interactive login first.

QNAP urges users to update Plex Media Server immediately, users should go to App Center, open My Apps and update Plex Media Server to version 1.43.3 or later. They should then check in Plex Web, under Settings and General, that the installed version is 1.43.3.10861 or later. QNAP will release further updates after verifying them, but users should not wait.

If Plex was reachable from the internet while running version 1.43.2 or earlier, users should treat the NAS as potentially compromised. This may apply if Plex Remote Access was enabled, port 32400 was forwarded, or the port was opened automatically through UPnP or router settings. Updating alone will not remove anything an attacker may have installed.

In those cases, users should follow QNAP’s FAQ to perform a clean reinstall, check for signs of compromise and reset both their Plex and NAS credentials. The company also advises disabling Plex Remote Access if it is not needed and avoiding port forwarding for port 32400. Users who need remote access should use a VPN instead.

QNAP also recommends keeping QTS or QuTS hero and all installed apps up to date. Step-by-step instructions are available in the Plex2Shell: Check and Remediation FAQ for QNAP NAS Users.

CISA added Plex2Shell flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 20, 2026, urging federal agencies to addresse them by October 23, 2026.

item.title: France Blames Iran for the Supermarket Fridge Attacks
item.description:
France blames Iran for supermarket fridge attacks. What’s known, what remains unclear, and how to secure exposed controllers.

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps was behind the attacks on supermarket fridges in France on 11 and 12 October. He said they hit 700 sites and raised refrigerator temperatures. Some stores threw away their entire stock of perishable food, and fires broke out in several.

“France attributes destabilization and sabotage campaigns against French interests to the Islamic Republic of Iran (electronic and cyber center of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of Iran – IRGC-ECC).” reads the announcement published by French cybersecurity agency ANSSI. “Following its investigation, C4 is able to attribute these destructive actions to the Shahid Kaveh cyber-offensive unit, affiliated with the electronic and cyber center of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of Iran (IRGC-ECC): infrastructure characteristics, use of signing tools, relay of the attack by a propaganda organ linked to Shahid Kaveh, traces of the use of Persian in the attack infrastructure.”

Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot described the attack as “unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression” and called it the first major cyber sabotage operation on French soil. He promised EU-level sanctions, and France summoned the Iranian ambassador. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the response should be strong, adding that she had only just learned about France’s attribution.

“I can confirm that this attack was carried out by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of the Islamic Republic of Iran,” Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said of the cyberattacks on French supermarkets, which occurred on October 11 and 12, and reported Le Monde.

“This attack is unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression,” said Barrot. “It marks the first large-scale cyberattack aimed at sabotage on our national territory, and it constitutes a major attack on the nation’s interests and the security of the French people.”

“We will implement sanctions at the European level against all those responsible,” he added.

Paris prosecutors opened a judicial investigation into the head of Shahid Kaveh, an offensive cyber unit tied to the Guards’ Electronic and Cyber Center, and his two deputies. Anyone else they identify can be added to the case.

The attribution cites shared infrastructure, attack tools, Persian-language traces, and amplification by a group-linked propaganda outlet.

French authorities say Iranian cyber operations targeting French interests date back to at least 2020. Previous incidents include a planned attack against Charlie Hebdo, a 2023 breach of its online store attributed to Emennet Pasargad, and a 2024 attempt to hijack digital advertising kiosks to display anti-Israel messages ahead of the Paris Olympics. C4 attributes these operations to the IRGC-linked Shahid Shoostari unit.

France wasn’t alone. On 2 November, supermarkets in at least nine other European countries reported a suspected attack on their freezer systems. Barrot spoke only about the French case, so nothing official yet ties the second wave to Iran.

This is where we need to be careful. When a government names a country as responsible for an attack, that’s a serious accusation. But the reports I’ve read don’t explain the technical evidence behind it. We should treat it as an official claim, not a proven fact, and stick to what we know. Fear and uncertainty can be used to spread distrust, and that risk applies to all sides involved in this story.


The key issue isn’t just identifying the attackers, but understanding whether someone is exploiting these incidents to promote a hybrid warfare narrative. Hacktivist claims may serve propaganda and visibility more than reflect actual responsibility. If French investigations confirm Iran’s role in the October attacks, the pro-Russian groups claiming November’s incidents could face a serious credibility problem. They may have tried to take credit for someone else’s operations. Still, their involvement in some incidents remains possible.

In today’s hybrid warfare, uncertain attribution, strategic ambiguity, and information manipulation make it increasingly difficult to separate real attacks from propaganda.

The method used in supermarket fridge attacks, at least, is documented. On 5 November, CISA, the FBI and other US agencies published a fact sheet on the same kind of activity. The actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards.

The agencies list three ways in: bypassing authentication, injecting code and weak settings. They also warn that operators can lose sight of the real temperatures, which is a bad thing to discover after the cheese has gone.

The fixes are dull and they work. Keep controllers off the internet, and if you need remote access, put an updated firewall in front of it. Separate industrial devices from the office network, change default passwords, add phishing-resistant multifactor authentication, patch firmware and replace devices the maker no longer supports.

Then limit who can change settings with an allowlist of approved devices and IP addresses. Keep tested backups offsite and offline, turn on logging and read the logs. The last control is the cheapest: Define and maintain reasonable setpoint limits for devices operating downstream of controllers to stay within safe ranges and establish alerting for deviations.

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Iran)

item.title: Iris Ohyama data breach may expose personal information of 7.7 million people
item.description:
Iris Ohyama warns that a cloud data breach may have exposed personal information of 7.7 million customers, including names and passwords.

Japanese household goods manufacturer Iris Ohyama has disclosed that attackers may have accessed personal information belonging to approximately 7.7 million people through an external cloud service used by its online shopping subsidiary, Iris Plaza. The incident highlights a security risk that often receives less attention than attacks against corporate networks: sensitive customer information can be exposed through services operated outside an organization’s own infrastructure.

Iris Plaza discovered a suspicious file in an external cloud service on October 28, 2026. The company immediately shut down its online shopping platform and related systems, launched an investigation and confirmed unauthorized access by a third party. It published an initial notification on October 29, followed by an update on November 5 detailing the potential impact.

In its official incident notice, the company confirmed that information stored in the external cloud environment may have been accessed or obtained by unauthorized parties.

“Iris Plaza Co., Ltd. (Headquarters: Sendai City, Miyagi Prefecture, President: Ryota Iwasaki, hereinafter referred to as “the Company”), a member of the Iris Group, has investigated the unauthorized access incident that occurred on its official online shopping site for Iris Ohyama, “Iris Plaza” (hereinafter referred to as “Iris Plaza”). As a result of the investigation, it has been determined that some personal information may have been leaked.” reads the company’s notice. “Subsequent investigations have confirmed the possibility that data stored on an external cloud service may have been leaked. The total amount of personal information stored was approximately 7.7 million records, and at this time, we have confirmed the possibility that this data may have been viewed or obtained. “

The 7.7 million figure refers to records stored in the affected cloud service, not confirmed stolen data. Potentially affected individuals include 5.8 million current and former members and 1.9 million non-members. Exposed information may include names, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, gender, dates of birth and passwords, some of which are encrypted.

“The following personal information may have been leaked at this time:

Not all of the above information about our customers has been leaked. The items affected vary depending on your registration status.” continues the notice. “Some items, including passwords, are encrypted.”

There is one important distinction: credit card information wasn’t stored in the affected cloud service and, according to the company, wasn’t exposed. Iris Plaza also says it hasn’t identified unauthorized access or data leaks involving its stores on other external e-commerce marketplaces. As of November 5, it had received no reports of fraudulent use of the information or financial losses linked to the incident. アイリスオーヤマ株式会社+1

The company reported the incident to Japanese police and the country’s Personal Information Protection Commission on October 29. It also blocked the unauthorized access route, suspended the affected systems and brought in external experts to support the investigation.

The response extended beyond the main shopping platform. Iris Plaza suspended its SIMPLE STYLE website, while another group company, Iris Tech Service, stopped its websites and new applications for home appliance subscriptions and furniture and appliance delivery and installation services. The company says it hasn’t found evidence that these additional services were compromised.

Iris Plaza has also warned customers about possible follow-up scams. Attackers could use the exposed personal information to create convincing phishing emails, SMS messages or phone calls, impersonating the company or other organizations. Fake websites and social media accounts could also appear, attempting to collect login credentials, payment details or other personal information.

The company is asking customers who reused their Iris Plaza passwords on other services to change them. It also says it will contact potentially affected individuals individually as the investigation progresses. Customers should be particularly careful with messages claiming to provide information about the incident, account recovery or compensation.

“We will never ask for your password, PIN, authentication code, or any other important information when we contact you.” アイリスオーヤマ株式会社

The incident is another reminder that organizations must extend security controls and monitoring beyond their own infrastructure. Third-party cloud services can hold millions of customer records, and unauthorized access to those environments can create consequences far beyond the service initially compromised.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Iris Ohyama)

item.title: Google fixes the eighth actively exploited Chrome zero-day of (2026)
item.description:
Google patched nine Chrome flaws, including a V8 vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-125350, that attackers have been actively exploiting in the wild.


Google has addressed multiple security vulnerabilities, one of which, tracked as CVE-2026-125350, has been actively exploited in the wild.

The vulnerability is a use after free issue that resides in XML and was reported by an anonymous source on November 6, 2026..

“Google is aware that an exploit for CVE-2026-125350 exists in the wild.” reads the advisory.

A Use-after-free (UAF) is a memory corruption vulnerability that occurs when a program continues to use a piece of memory after it has been released (freed).

In simple terms, an application allocates memory to store data, then releases that memory when it is no longer needed. A use-after-free bug occurs when the application later tries to access that same memory location, even though it is no longer valid.

Attackers may exploit a use-after-free vulnerability to crash an application and cause a denial-of-service condition, corrupt memory, or, under certain conditions, execute arbitrary code. Depending on the affected component and the nature of the flaw, successful exploitation could also allow attackers to escalate their privileges.

The IT giant has not shared further details about how attackers are exploiting the vulnerability or who is behind the attacks.

“Access to bug details and links may be kept restricted until a majority of users are updated with a fix. We will also retain restrictions if the bug exists in a third party library that other projects similarly depend on, but haven’t yet fixed.” continues the advisory.

CVE-2026-125350 is the eighth exploited Chrome zero-day of 2026. Since the start of the year, Google has addressed the following zero-day flaws exploited in attacks in the wild:

Google has released Chrome 157.0.8103.50/.51 for Windows and Mac and 157.0.8103.50 for Linux. The update will roll out gradually over the coming days and weeks.

item.title: iOS Sandbox Escape Is Public, and Apple Hasn’t Confirmed a Fix
item.description:
A public iOS sandbox escape could expose wallet keys, Binance warns. No attacks are reported and no fix is confirmed.

On 10 November, Binance warned users about a public iOS sandbox escape that lets one app read the files of other apps. Seed phrases, private keys and login credentials could be exposed to a malicious app, the exchange said.

“A vulnerability (worse_query) affecting iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1, and 27.2 allows malicious apps to read local files from other apps, putting seed phrases, private keys, and login credentials at risk across the entire ecosystem. This is an iOS-level issue, not unique to Binance.” reads the warning.

Binance advises users to remove apps installed from untrusted sources, update iOS and all apps to the latest official versions, and, if a breach is suspected, move funds to a new wallet on a clean device and reset all active login sessions.

A researcher known as ‘forcequitOS’ published the PoC exploit code, called worse_query, on GitHub. Apple released security updates for both iOS versions the following day, but its release notes mysteriously don’t report a fix for the issue. The good news is that neither Binance nor the researcher has reported any attacks or data theft.

“worse_query is the direct successor to bad_query and essentially replaces it. To use worse_query, you’ll have to set up an App Group container for your app.” forcequitOS wrote.

item.title: Russia-Linked APT Turla Turned Exchange Servers Into Their Own Control Room
item.description:
ESET found Russia-Linked APT group Turla using a new toolset, dubbed Cereal, on government Exchange servers in Kazakhstan and Romania.

ESET Research detailed a previously undocumented toolset it calls Cereal, built to run on Microsoft Exchange servers. The researchers found it on 28 November 2025 at a government body in Kazakhstan, and later at a government body in Romania, which was compromised on 23 December. The researchers discovered that in Romania, it was set up to spot emails to or from NATO and the European Union. ESET attributes it with high confidence to the Turla APT group (aka Secret Blizzard, Snake, Uroburos, Waterbug, Venomous Bear and KRYPTON) that has been active since at least 2004, targeting diplomatic and government organizations and private businesses in the Middle East, Asia, Europe, North and South America, and former Soviet bloc nations.

According to the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), the Russia-nexus actor is assessed to be affiliated with Center 16 of Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB).

The name Cereal comes from serialization, a process that programs use to package data and code for transfer. Most of the toolset consists of modular .NET code that arrives encrypted, unpacks itself in memory and leaves almost no files on disk. Only the first loader is saved as a regular .NET file.

One unusual feature is that ESET found no attacker-controlled server. The main backdoor, CerealNeuron, doesn’t connect to an external server. Instead, it runs on the victim’s Exchange server and waits for commands through web paths that look like normal Outlook Web Access, Autodiscover and ActiveSync traffic. This makes the activity difficult to spot in firewall logs. If a request isn’t properly encrypted or fails security checks, the server simply returns a normal-looking Exchange error page.

“CerealNeuron, a passive backdoor with no built-in commands but capable of executing assemblies contained in CerealRunner binaries, received in network requests;” reads the analysis published by ESET.

“The consequences are significant:

  • Malicious traffic coexists with legitimate Exchange web services – exactly the kind of traffic defenders are least likely to block.”
  • There is no dedicated C&C infrastructure to discover, block, or take down. The victim’s own internet-facing Exchange server is the operator-accessible control point.
  • Network-based tracking is severely limited. We were unable to identify the ingress IP addresses used by the operators. They may have connected directly, via anonymization services, or from other compromised hosts.”

As a result, defenders have no external server to block or take down. ESET couldn’t even identify the attackers’ IP addresses. A second version, called CerealHermit, has no network functions and reads encrypted command files directly from disk. This means some victims had two separate ways for attackers to access their systems.

Commands work like disposable programs. Instead of one backdoor with a built-in menu, the operators send each task as a small compiled .NET program carried by a component called CerealRunner. The tasks include pulling mailboxes through Exchange Web Services, querying Active Directory, running WMI queries, extracting locally stored Windows credentials and handling files. ESET saw so many near-identical binaries that it believes the operators run an internal system that builds them automatically.

The .NET tricks are what set this apart. The first loader abuses a rarely used feature to run native code before any .NET code, so an analyst sees an entry point that does nothing. Operators also dropped it into the Windows management folder under names like ncobjapi.dll, and into the .NET native image cache under names like Microsoft.Exchange.Search.Mdb.ni.dll, so trusted processes loaded it for them.

The email theft is the part ESET calls new. The module, CerealBox, injects itself into EdgeTransport.exe, the process that handles mail flow, and wraps the handlers of transport agents already running in memory.

“CerealBox uses a stealthier approach. Instead of registering itself, it is injected directly into EdgeTransport.exe, the Exchange process that handles email flow.” continues the report. “Reaching that point, however, is not straightforward: CerealBox is delivered through an intricate chain of nested Cereal components”

It registers no new agent, so nothing shows up in Exchange’s configuration. A message qualifies if it carries a .doc, .docx or .pdf file and matches hardcoded lists of senders, recipients, subject words or file names. Selected messages get compressed, encrypted and staged on disk, and the operators collect and delete them later.

The victims match Turla’s usual targets. According to ESET, around 70% of the countries targeted by the group since 2022 were former Soviet republics or European countries that once had close ties with Moscow. The focus on Romanian NATO and EU email systems is consistent with Russia’s long-standing intelligence interests. ESET also links the attacks in Kazakhstan to the country’s deportation of Russian exiles since January 2026. Activity in the country increased on January 15, the day after the Old New Year holiday.

Organizations running Exchange should check for suspicious activity that may not be visible in standard configurations. This includes unusual DLL files in the Windows management folder, unexpected files in the native image cache and suspicious requests to the three web paths used by the backdoor. A clean list of Exchange transport agents does not necessarily mean that the mail system is free from compromise.

“The Cereal toolset is a carefully constructed instrument for long-term, stealthy cyberespionage.” concludes the report. “The Cereal toolset demonstrates that, for Turla, Exchange servers are not just mail servers – they are durable collection points, internal execution hubs, and a suitable environment for hiding sophisticated .NET tradecraft.”

item.title: U.S. CISA adds IBM, SignalWire FreeSwitch, OpenSSH, and GPUStack flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog
item.description:
U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) adds IBM, SignalWire FreeSwitch, OpenSSH, and GPUStack flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added IBM, SignalWire FreeSwitch, OpenSSH, and GPUStack vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog:

Below are the flaws added to the catalog:

  • CVE-2026-102895 GPUStack Improper Authentication Vulnerability 
  • CVE-2026-116779 SignalWire FreeSwitch Code Injection Vulnerability 
  • CVE-2026-123158 OpenBSD OpenSSH Unexpected Status Code or Return Value Vulnerability 
  • CVE-2026-123218 IBM Aspera Faspex Incorrect Authorization Vulnerability 

The first issue added to the catalog, CVE-2026-102895 (CVSS score of 9.8), is an improper authentication vulnerability affecting GPUStack, an open-source platform used to manage GPU clusters and AI model deployments. The flaw allows remote, unauthenticated attackers to bypass authentication and obtain administrator privileges by making requests appear to originate from the local system. Successful exploitation can expose sensitive information, create persistent administrator API keys, modify configurations and potentially execute arbitrary code. Exploitation has been observed in the wild against a GPUStack 2.1.1 deployment. Security researcher Javier Sixto reported the in-the-wild exploitation, but no specific threat group has been identified. The issue affects versions before 2.2.0.

The second issue, CVE-2026-116779 (CVSS score of 9.8), is a code injection vulnerability in SignalWire FreeSWITCH, an open-source communications platform. The flaw allows attackers to send specially crafted SIP MESSAGE requests and abuse the API chat protocol to execute FreeSWITCH API commands. Depending on the configuration, this can expose credentials and configuration data, manipulate telephone calls and execute operating system commands with the privileges of the FreeSWITCH process. SignalWire confirmed that exploitation has been observed in the wild. The vulnerability was added to CISA’s KEV catalog on November 9, 2026, but no information identifying the attackers or a specific campaign has been disclosed. FreeSWITCH versions before 1.11.3 are affected.

The third issue, CVE-2026-123158 (CVSS score of 8.1), is an authentication bypass vulnerability affecting OpenSSH. Under specific conditions, when OpenSSH runs on Linux systems using the musl C library without Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM), the SSH server may incorrectly interpret password input as a password hash. A remote, unauthenticated attacker can exploit the flaw by submitting a specially crafted password to bypass authentication and access affected accounts. CISA added the vulnerability to its KEV catalog on November 6, 2026, indicating that exploitation has been observed. However, no specific threat actor or attack campaign has been publicly identified. OpenSSH versions before 10.6p2 are affected.

The fourth issue, CVE-2026-123218 (CVSS score of 9.8), is an incorrect authorization vulnerability affecting IBM Aspera Faspex 5. It allows an authenticated user to craft a specific message that bypasses authorization checks and potentially gain full administrative privileges. Successful exploitation could give attackers access to sensitive information and allow them to modify or disrupt the affected system. IBM disclosed the vulnerability on November 7, 2026, and released a fix in Aspera Faspex 5.0.19 PL1. I found no public confirmation of exploitation in the wild or information identifying attackers at the time of writing. Versions 5.0.0 through 5.0.19 are affected.

According to Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 22-01: Reducing the Significant Risk of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities, FCEB agencies have to address the identified vulnerabilities by the due date to protect their networks against attacks exploiting the flaws in the catalog.

Experts also recommend that private organizations review the Catalog and address the vulnerabilities in their infrastructure.

CISA orders federal agencies to fix the two vulnerabilities by November 12, 2026.

item.title: Microsoft November Patch Tuesday: one exploited Outlook bug and 30 wormable flaws
item.description:
Microsoft November Patch Tuesday security updates fix 1,090 flaws, including one exploited Outlook bug and 30 potentially wormable issues.

Microsoft November Patch Tuesday addressed about 1,090 new vulnerabilities, which is less than the roughly 1,400 last month. Two months in a row now exceed every previous year from Microsoft, and the overall count is a bit confusing, so other trackers report different totals.

The release covers Windows and its components, Office, networking and remote access, graphics, media and printing, storage and file systems, .NET and Visual Studio, security and identity, Azure and cloud, Exchange Server, Dynamics and Xbox. Only one bug is under active attack and none is publicly known. ZDI says that doesn’t mean less exploitation, only fewer zero-days, and it guesses that AI is better at reversing patches than at finding and exploiting bugs in closed-source software.

The exploited bug is CVE-2026-124194, an Outlook spoofing flaw, and its name undersells the impact. An attacker sends a crafted message file and talks the user into opening it, and Outlook connects to an attacker-controlled location without the usual external-content warning, which leaks the user’s NTLMv2 hash.

“An unauthenticated attacker could send a specially crafted message file and convince a user to open it in an affected version of Microsoft Outlook. Opening the file could cause Outlook to connect to an attacker-controlled network location without displaying the usual external-content warning, potentially disclosing authentication information that could be used to impersonate the user. Exploitation requires network connectivity and user interaction.” reads the advisory. “An attacker must send a user a malicious Office file and convince them to open it.”

The attacker can then authenticate as that user. The Preview Pane isn’t an attack path and the CVSS score is only 6.5, but ZDI says to put it first because Microsoft marks it as exploited.

CVE-2026-116928 is a Windows Search remote code execution bug reached through Exchange Server. An unauthenticated attacker emails a crafted attachment, and the bug triggers when the server indexes it automatically, so the recipient never opens anything. It’s zero-click, scores CVSS 9.8, and ZDI rates it more severe than any of the nine patches Exchange gets this month.

CVE-2026-119958 hits the Windows LDAP service. An unauthenticated attacker sends crafted LDAP calls over the network, triggers an out-of-bounds write and runs code in the service context, which could be destructive on domain controllers. ZDI says to test and deploy it quickly. CVE-2026-119952, a Schannel remote code execution flaw, is marked “Exploitation More Likely”, one of only a few Critical patches with that rating, and its high attack complexity is why the score is lower.

CVE-2026-119990, an Azure OpenAI elevation of privilege bug, got a bulletin that said “Customer Action Required: Yes” and then listed nothing to do. An unauthenticated attacker could send a crafted request over the internet and reach orchestration information, change workflows or disrupt the service. Microsoft has since revised it to say no customer action is needed. A bulletin that says action required and lists none is the most relaxed urgent notice you’ll read this month.

Two more stand out for their components. CVE-2026-95962 is a use-after-free in the little-documented Windows Virtual Filtering Platform, reachable with a crafted network packet and needing no authentication or user interaction. It involves a race condition, but ZDI notes those get beaten all the time at Pwn2Own. CVE-2026-112967 is a heap overflow in the Xbox Live Networking Service with a CVSS of 9.8, and ZDI doesn’t think exploitation is likely but enjoys imagining Xbox Live exploits in the wild.

ZDI counts 30 wormable bugs this month, down from 59 last month. Seventeen carry advisory wording about an unauthenticated attacker running code over the network with no interaction, and 13 use variant wording or have no FAQ but show the same pattern in their summaries and CVSS vectors. ZDI warns it may be wrong on some, since a few advisories are light on detail.

Network-facing services like DNS, DHCP, LDAP and Exchange deserve the earliest attention.

“I may be wrong about some of these, since a few advisories are light on detail.” concludes ZDI. “As always, I recommend testing and deploying these patches quickly, especially for network-facing services like DNS, DHCP, LDAP, and Exchange”

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Patch Tuesday)

item.title: Hackers Advertise a $1,000 Gmail Tool That Allegedly Survives Password Resets
item.description:
Hackers advertise a $1,000-a-month tool claiming persistent Gmail access after password resets, but its effectiveness remains unverified.

A developer of hacking tools is selling a $1,000 per month feature that allegedly gives criminals continuous access to Gmail inboxes. The cybersecurity firm Hudson Rock reports that the tool can keep reading a victim’s mailbox after a password change, after the browser closes and after sessions are revoked.

“Remus Stealer is advertising a way for criminals to open a compromised Gmail inbox directly from a stolen-device record.” reads the report published by cybersecurity firm Hudson Rock. “Its latest pitch goes further: the operator claims access continues even after the victim changes their password or revokes sessions.”

The tool belongs to Remus Stealer, an infostealer, meaning malware that steals data from infected computers. Remus supposedly gives its operators a searchable inbox right inside a stolen-device dashboard. Hudson Rock says it spoke with the developer and with a customer who used it, and the customer supplied screenshots of messages, timestamps and a control for sharing a mailbox with other operators.

If the claims are true, the risk goes beyond a single Gmail inbox. Attackers could read password reset links and verification codes, allowing them to access other accounts linked to that email address. This makes Gmail a valuable target because many online services use it to recover accounts.

“In the supplied , Remus promotes email-code interception without collecting browser cookie files, claims that password changes and session revocation do not stop it, and advertises shareable mailbox links. The feature is listed as Enterprise-only; the advertises that tier at $1,000 per month.” continues the report. “The sharing claim concerns giving other operators access to an already acquired mailbox through the service. The material does not show a victim being infected by opening one of those links.”

It is still unclear how the tool works. Hudson Rock says Remus does not steal browser cookies, while its developer claims that changing the Gmail password does not stop access. The developer has not shared technical details. He only said that the malware interacts with browser memory, but this does not explain how it can maintain access after a password change or when active sessions are revoked.

Hudson Rock believes Remus may obtain or create an authorization token while the victim is logged into Gmail through a browser. A remote component could then use this authorization to access emails even after the malware has stopped running, as long as Google continues to accept it. Tom’s Guide also reports that the tool can bypass Google’s anti-fraud checks and says it has contacted Google for comment.

However, other reports highlight some important uncertainties. CyberInsider says Hudson Rock has not confirmed that the tool can maintain access after a password change, nor has it established that the feature exploits a Gmail vulnerability. Hudson Rock has not conducted a controlled test to show that Remus can still access newly received emails after the victim changes their password and revokes existing sessions and third-party access. According to Cybernews, the developer describes the feature as a Gmail “zero-day”. However, this claim has not been independently reproduced.

The business side is more concrete. CyberInsider says the mailbox feature sits in an Enterprise tier at $1,000 per month, with shareable mailbox links so criminals can hand an inbox they’ve already compromised to others. The actor behind Remus Stealer offers the MaaS with three subscription tiers: Basic at $250, Pro at $500 and Enterprise at $1,000.

This kind of claim has a history. In late 2023, a developer called PRISMA surfaced an exploit that regenerated persistent Google cookies by manipulating a token and account ID pair, and Lumma then used it so access continued after a password reset. It’s a precedent and not proof, since Remus’ mechanism is unknown, and Hudson Rock still treats a Google password change as an essential recovery step, while saying victims should also look for other ways an attacker could keep access.

The tool is marketed to “enterprise” customers, so most users are unlikely to be targeted. It will probably be used mainly against organizations and high-profile individuals. Hudson Rock recommends that victims first disconnect and clean the infected computer before accessing their trusted accounts again. They should then change compromised passwords using a clean device and review their signed-in devices to remove suspicious sessions and third-party access.

Hudson Rock also advises users to check Gmail settings for unauthorized changes and secure any other accounts that use the compromised mailbox for password resets or verification codes. Other basic precautions remain important: watch out for phishing emails with urgent messages, spelling mistakes or suspicious sender addresses, and keep antivirus software up to date. Tom’s Guide expects Google to introduce additional Gmail protections if the tool proves as effective as its developer claims.

For now, this is a vendor’s marketing claim supported by customer screenshots and Hudson Rock’s investigation, not a confirmed Gmail vulnerability. One important detail offers some reassurance: attackers must first infect the victim’s computer and compromise their mailbox before they can use the tool.

“Remus is marketing an integrated mailbox-reading capability, and a customer has endorsed its claimed persistence. The most plausible broad model is reuse of access obtained or established during endpoint compromise.” concludes the report. “The evidence does not identify the mechanism or show fresh mail remaining accessible after comprehensive recovery.”

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Gmail)

item.title: WhiteArmor Demands $5 Million from Maersk, Claims Theft of 100GB of Data
item.description:
Maersk confirms a data breach involving a legacy system, while WhiteArmor claims 100GB of stolen data and demands a $5 million ransom.

A.P. Moller Maersk, the Danish shipping giant, says it identified an IT security incident involving unauthorized access and data extraction from one of its local legacy systems, one inherited from a previous acquisition.

“Maersk has identified an IT security incident involving unauthorised access and data extraction from one of our local legacy systems from a previous acquisition.” reads the statement published by Maersk on November 11. “Our findings so far strongly suggest no sensitive data has been disclosed. The incident is isolated to a local system, and we have found no indication that there has been any impact on other Maersk systems or customer and partner systems that connect to Maersk through integrations such as APIs and EDI.”

According to Maersk, its cyber security team started a full investigation as soon as it found the problem, and it’s still going. The company says swift action secured the affected system. Its findings so far strongly suggest no sensitive data has been disclosed, and it says the incident is isolated to that one local system.

Maersk has found no sign that other Maersk systems were affected, or the customer and partner systems that connect to it through integrations such as APIs and EDI. It doesn’t expect disruption for customers, who can book and manage shipments as usual. It promises updates and says it will inform any affected parties if it finds a need to.

Maersk didn’t name the system, the type of data or the date of the intrusion. However, the cybercrime group WhiteArmor added the company to its Tor data leak site:

WhiteArmor demanded a $5 million ransom in Bitcoin, giving Maersk 30 days to pay. The group claims to have stolen about 100 GB of data from the OCF/LF Logistics platform, which supports logistics and supply chain operations.

“”Your contract-logistics arm, the former LF Logistics, runs fulfilment for many of the world’s largest consumer brands,” states the leak site. “Five million dollars is roughly four hours of that EBITDA.””

Maersk acquired LF Logistics, the company that developed the platform, from the Li & Fung Group in 2022. This could match Maersk’s reference to an old system inherited through an acquisition, although the company has not confirmed this connection.

According to the attackers, the stolen data includes nearly 30,000 driver records, passwords stored in plain text, 33 super admin accounts and signed delivery receipts. The group also claims to have stolen inventory records, purchase orders, advance shipping notices and 27,842 mobile device logs containing phone numbers, email addresses and IMEI numbers. These details come from the attackers and have not been independently verified. Maersk’s statement does not confirm their claims. WhiteArmor also tried to justify its demand, saying the $5 million ransom represents roughly four hours of revenue for the logistics business.

“We do not anticipate disruption to operations for customers at this time, and customers can continue to use Maersk platforms to book and manage their shipments as usual.” concludes the statement. “We will keep customers updated as more relevant information becomes available, and if we identify any need to inform impacted parties of any further findings, we will do so.”

The scale of Maersk’s operations explains why this incident matters. A.P. Moller-Maersk is one of the world’s largest integrated shipping and logistics companies, playing a major role in global trade and supply chains. It operates around 700 container ships, representing approximately 13.5% of global container fleet capacity, and manages 60 terminals across 35 countries. The company employs about 100,000 people in 130 countries and provides services covering ocean shipping, port operations, warehousing, customs clearance and end-to-end supply chain management.

Maersk reported approximately $54 billion in revenue and $2.9 billion in net profit in 2025. Its global reach and reliance on interconnected IT systems make cybersecurity a major concern. A breach involving even an older, locally operated platform could expose sensitive business and personal information, including data belonging to drivers, customers and logistics partners, even if the company’s main systems remain unaffected.

In 2017, NotPetya forced the company to reinstall more than 4,000 servers and 45,000 workstations from scratch. It operated without IT for ten days and took damages of up to $300 million.

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, ransomware)
